newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Peacekeepers move tanks against Liberia rebels.
newsitem.headline: Peacekeepers move tanks against Liberia rebels.

text.p: Truckloads of African peacekeepers backed by tanks rolled into western Liberia on Wednesday to clear out guerrillas blocking highways to international relief workers, witnesses said.
A spokesman for the Nigerian-led ECOMOG force, Major Patrick Okoh, said the troops encountered no rebels as they swept into the hinterland from the capital Monrovia.
Peacekeepers would continue patrols in the area, he said.
The operation followed a deadline by ECOMOG commander General Victor Malu for rebels of Roosevelt Johnson's ULIMO-J militia to remove roadblocks in Cape Mount and Bomi counties.
"ECOMOG troops who patrolled the highways today saw no sign of armed men or roadblocks. Perhaps they had fled the area before the deadline expired," ECOMOG's Okoh said.
"We do not expect resistance, but if that happens it would be unfortunate," Okoh told Reuters.
Hundreds of frightened and starving villagers, including many who had sheltered in the bush to escape rampaging rebels, emerged to welcome the troops, reporters in the convoy said.
Continuing clashes around the western town of Tubmanburg have again threatened the latest accord to end more than six years of civil war in Liberia.
Troops of the ECOMOG force in 16 trucks earlier sang war songs and waved their weapons as they left Monrovia through the Po River bridge.
ULIMO-J spokesman Madison Wion said on state radio as the operation began that his men would not resist ECOMOG, but he pleaded for time for them to withdraw.
Fighting between ECOMOG and ULIMO-J in the area last December and January was followed by militia warfare in Monrovia in April and May that derailed a 1995 peace accord.
Fear of a repeat of those battles increased after tough comments by General Malu on Wednesday.

"We have ordered our troops to return fire if shot at first," he told British Broadcasting Corporation radio. "Knowing the faction we are dealing with we'll take no chances in Cape Mount and Tubmanburg."
Okoh said the troops would split into two groups and simultaneously head for Cape Mount to the west and the ULIMO-J stronghold town of Tubmanburg.
A West African summit in Nigeria last August pressured Liberia's squabbling warlords to sign a new accord providing for disarament of 60,000 guerrillas and elections by May next year.
Despite symbolic gestures and promises of disarmament, the process has yet to take off in earnest as ECOMOG says it is waiting for troop reinforcements from regional states.
Militia clashes have meanwhile broken out in parts of the country, notably in the west where aid workers have been prevented from distributing food aid to starving people.
More than 150,000 people have died in the conflict in Liberia, which was founded by freed American slaves in 1847 as Africa's first independent republic.
The U.S. military helped evacuate foreigners at the height of the fighting in Monrovia in April and May and marines backed by warships helped protect the American embassy.
